data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The single dominant cross-city modulator is city size itself: larger cities accumulate more stored thermal mass in their impervious surfaces and generate more anthropogenic heat, creating a mesoscale heat dome whose nocturnal temperature gap scales with the spatial extent of the urbanized area.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If small dense cities show larger nocturnal UHI than large sprawling cities, city size alone cannot be the modulator","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the nocturnal UHI correlates more strongly with building height density than with spatial extent, city size is a proxy rather than the causal variable","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If mesoscale simulations show that the heat dome effect saturates at small city sizes, the scaling argument fails","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the per-area heat storage is identical across city sizes but the UHI differs, the mechanism driving variation is not total thermal mass but surface properties or geometry","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Urban surfaces with high heat capacity and thermal mass store solar energy during the day and release it as sensible heat after sunset. A larger city has greater total impervious surface area, more thermal mass, and more anthropogenic emissions. On clear, calm nights, the lack of advection means this heat dome is not ventilated, and the integrated heat storage over a larger area creates a deeper, more persistent nocturnal warm layer. The nocturnal UHI gap therefore scales with city size: larger cities produce larger nighttime temperature differences.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
